What about his miracles

Same deal — one real phenomenon, mundane mechanisms underneath.

The famous one is Alexei's hemophilia, especially the 1912 Spala crisis, where Rasputin telegrammed from Siberia that the boy would live and the bleeding stopped after the doctors had given up. The forensic reads:

- **He told them to keep the doctors away.** Royal physicians were dosing Alexei with aspirin, which thins blood — the standard remedy then, actively harmful for a hemophiliac. Withdrawing it lets clotting resume.
- **He calmed the room.** Bleeding severity tracks blood pressure and agitation; a screaming child with a panicking mother bleeds worse. Rasputin's whole method was stillness and authority — the one intervention that actually helps hemorrhage.
- **Selection bias.** He was summoned to many crises. The hits became scripture; the misses were forgotten, and he was reportedly careful about which sickbeds he attended.

The Siberian peasant-healer reputation is the same stack: folk remedies, charisma, and illnesses that resolve on their own getting credited to whoever was in the room. No documented case needs the supernatural once you account for aspirin, adrenaline, and who wrote the history.
Wait you said stillness and authority. Explain

The mechanism is physiological, not mystical.

A hemophiliac child in a bleeding crisis is in pain and terrified — screaming, thrashing, heart rate and blood pressure spiking. That actively worsens hemorrhage: higher pressure pushes more blood out, and agitation prevents any clot from forming. Alexandra's panic fed his panic in a loop, and a cluster of anxious doctors hovering and probing kept the whole room at maximum arousal.

Rasputin's move was environmental. He'd clear the room or command stillness, sit with the boy, pray quietly, lay hands on him. Low stimulation, slow voice, physical calm. Heart rate drops, blood pressure drops, the bleeding slows enough for what clotting capacity the boy had to actually work. It's the single most effective non-pharmacological intervention for hemorrhage, and it looks like a miracle because nobody else in that palace could produce calm — they were all terrified of the Tsarina's terror.

The authority part is what made it possible. He wasn't suggesting; he was commanding the Empress of Russia to sit down and be quiet, and she obeyed. That authority did double duty: it cleared the room (removing the agitation source) and it stopped the aspirin (removing the iatrogenic harm). His "power" over the boy's body was really power over the adults around the boy — the only lever that mattered.

Reading "audible" as "ordeal" — the Alexander I vs. Napoleon saga. Broadly yes, it's one of the best-documented personal rivalries in history:

- **Tilsit, 1807:** they met on a raft in the middle of the Neman River — neutral ground, literally floating between their armies — and Napoleon charmed Alexander into an alliance. Alexander reportedly told him "I hate the English as much as you do." Real, documented by both courts.
- **Erfurt, 1808:** the follow-up summit, where Talleyrand — Napoleon's own foreign minister — secretly pulled Alexander aside and told him to resist Napoleon. Also real, confirmed in memoirs on both sides.
- **The break:** the Continental System was wrecking Russia's economy, and Napoleon's marriage snub (picked Marie Louise of Austria over a Russian grand duchess) stung. By 1812 Alexander was done.
- **1812–1814:** the invasion, the burning of Moscow, the retreat — then Alexander personally leading the coalition into Paris in March 1814 and insisting on abdication over a negotiated peace.

The one legendary bit is the ending: Alexander died mysteriously in Taganrog in 1825, and the rumor that he faked his death and became the Siberian hermit Feodor Kuzmich persisted for a century. Never proven, never quite killed either.

You're compressing two real events into one, and the compression is doing interesting work.

**The "stormed in instead of waiting" part is Austerlitz, December 1805.** Alexander — 27, no battlefield experience — overruled Kutuzov, who wanted to fall back east and wait for reinforcements (Austrian forces under Archduke Charles marching up from Italy, plus a second Russian army). Alexander attacked Napoleon on a field Napoleon had chosen. Catastrophe.

**The "terrible peace" part is Tilsit, 1807** — but it wasn't Alexander's peace that was terrible, it was Britain's. After Friedland, Alexander cut a separate deal with Napoleon and left Britain — the ally bankrolling the coalitions — completely hung out to dry. London read it as betrayal.

Two corrections to the details: "Austro-Hungarian" is a half-century early (Austria-Hungary doesn't exist until 1867 — in 1805 it's just Austria), and Britain wasn't sending battalions to that theater. Their contribution was the navy and the money. The battalions Alexander should have waited for were Austrian and Russian.

I knew it 


Had Napoleon been successful in Russia, the rest of Europe's Great Powers would have just waited for the next opportunity. But when the French started losing to Russia, most of Europe sprang into action. The plan was for every major European army to advance on Paris at a steady pace, but to pull back whenever opposed by the French army. The allies knew that they couldn't defeat Napoleon on the battlefield, but with all of Europe's armies advancing as one, they wouldn't have to. Napoleon couldn't be everywhere at once. Even if he won every possible battle, the allies would still take Paris. The point is that no one country defeated Napoleon. Every country defeated Napoleon. But Tsar Alexander didn't see it like this. In his mind, it was all his doing. As part of their plan, the allies had developed lists of key French towns to capture on the way to Paris. The allied armies would need their logistical support, especially with several French armies coming up behind them. Tsar Alexander was personally in command of the Russian army, and once he was within spitting distance of French territory, he abandoned this plan and broke off from his allies and advanced on Paris alone. Alexander later said that this was a matter of personal honour.
He had made a commitment to his people that there would be Russian soldiers marching down the streets of Paris. Never mind the commitment he made to his allies to all advance as one. Apparently personal honour can only go so far. It was Tsar Alexander of Russia who took Paris, and it was Tsar Alexander who accepted Napoleon's surrender. Since Alexander placed himself in the center of the action, the fact that he liked to tell conflicting narratives about himself suddenly became very important to world history. On one hand, Alexander styled himself as the grand enemy of the French, as Napoleon finally meeting his match on the field of battle. On the other hand, Alexander still believed that he was the honourable man in Europe. Spin the randomizer and what do we get? Honour. Today, Alexander would treat Napoleon not as the enemy of Europe, but as his equal. The Emperor of Russia meeting with the Emperor of France. It was as equals that Alexander negotiated Napoleon's surrender, and as equals, Alexander gave Napoleon almost everything he wanted. Napoleon would be allowed to retain the title of Emperor, and would be permitted to remain an independent monarch until his death, ruling over the small island of Elba off the coast of Italy.
He wouldn't be allowed to leave, but on the island he would be a free man. The allies were apoplectic. This was not what they had agreed to. This put the British in particular in a terrible position, since they had deliberately never recognized Napoleon as the legitimate Emperor of France. Now, for some reason, the Russian Tsar was forcing them to legitimize Napoleon only in defeat. It was humiliating. When the rest of the allies arrived in Paris, several of their leaders got up in Alexander's face and went ballistic. Alexander was in a different mood that day, and gave them a placid response, saying that it was his duty, as a Christian, to forgive his enemies. This is what made Alexander impossible to deal with. Today he was saying that Napoleon had to remain an Emperor for religious reasons. Yesterday it was because of honour and tradition. Tomorrow? Who knows! The Austrian Foreign Minister summarized these events in a report to his monarch, in which he called Alexander, (this is a real quote,) "the biggest baby on earth." He continued, "he has started out by doing a great deal of harm. We have repaired some of it, but we will suffer for some time as a result of the things he got up to in those first moments when he ran away from us!" Alexander's stated priorities going into the peace conference kinda depended on his mood, but it mostly had to do with the future of France.
As previously discussed, the allies had all agreed to restore the old Bourbon dynasty to the French throne. The problem was that Alexander didn't like the Bourbon kings. If you look at France's position in Europe, France had an interest in making sure that central Europe remained fragmented and weak, and outside of the influence of any other Great Power. To these ends, France had a long history of aligning itself with countries like Poland and Saxony and the Ottoman Empire. This was of course a geopolitical thing, but Tsar Alexander thought that it was a personal thing, and that the Bourbon kings uniquely had a problem with Russia. Alexander's immediate priority was to keep the Bourbon Louis XVIII off of the French throne. He suggested making Napoleon's 4 year old son the king of France, but Talleyrand patiently explained to him that this would allow Napoleon to pull the strings from exile. Alexander then tried to put a man named Bernadotte on the French throne. Bernadotte was a former French marshall who had turned against Napoleon, and was singlehandedly responsible for bringing Sweden into the coalition against France. In the late stages of the war Bernadotte and Alexander had worked closely together, and Alexander viewed him as the one Frenchman that he could trust.
Alexander pushed hard for Bernadotte, but Talleyrand wouldn't budge. He and the allies had all agreed to a Bourbon restoration, and they all saw Bernadotte for what he was. An attempt to put a Russian puppet on the French throne. Talleyrand explained to Alexander that they couldn't be placing whomever they wished on the French throne, or they were no better than the Revolutionaries. The new king needed to be a legitimate French king of royal blood. Alexander got desperate. What about a distant cousin? A younger brother? Anybody but Louis XVIII. Talleyrand held firm, and Alexander backed down. An impressive feat, considering that the Russians had Paris under military occupation. A Bourbon king would return to the French throne, and Alexander's dream of a grand Franco-Russian alliance withered and died. I mentioned the Austrian Foreign Minister before, and how he had a rather dim opinion of the Russian Tsar. "Biggest baby on earth," and all that. The Austrian Foreign Minister's name was Klemens von Metternich, and the period we're beginning to cover today is sometimes called "The Age of Metternich." That's a clue as to his importance. Metternich would become the architect of the postwar international system, and one of the 19th century's most preeminent figures.

Is the video’s framing of the impact of that event well founded?

Yes, with one dramatization. Checking the pieces:

**Solid:**
- The "biggest baby on earth" quote is real. Metternich wrote that if he'd reached Paris a few days earlier he'd have stopped Alexander, "the biggest baby on earth," from acting "like a schoolboy who has escaped from his teacher" — corroborated in Mark Braude's *The Invisible Emperor*, which draws on the same sources the video cites.
- The Fontainebleau terms were drawn up without the other allies. Metternich, Castlereagh, and Hardenberg only arrived in Paris on April 10, found the deal done, signed under protest. Britain refused full signature precisely because it had never recognized Napoleon as emperor — Castlereagh filed a limited accession instead.
- The terms were objectively generous: retains the imperial title, sovereign Elba, 2 million francs a year, a personal guard. And Metternich's prediction that they'd be back at war within two years was vindicated by the Hundred Days — the video's impact framing (this decision directly enabled Napoleon's return) is the mainstream read.
- Alexander floating Bernadotte and the King of Rome as alternatives to Louis XVIII is documented — the Cambridge international-law piece on Fontainebleau notes he was still unimpressed with Louis and had considered a regency.

**The dramatization:** "advanced on Paris alone" is overstated. Blücher's Prussians fought at the Battle of Paris too — Alexander didn't literally ride in solo. What he did unilaterally was seize the *negotiations*: the surrender terms were his personal deal with Napoleon, presented to the other allies as a fait accompli. The video compresses the military and diplomatic unilateralism into one gesture. The substance — he cut his allies out of the endgame — survives the correction.
